#6415. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6414. A New Light-Powered Quantum Processor Could Overcome a Major Computing Barrier

A new light-based processor suggests future quantum computers could tackle very different problems without being rebuilt, while laying the groundwork for more reliable calculations.

Light has enormous potential for quantum computing, but one of its greatest strengths is also a major obstacle. Photons, the tiny particles that make up light, are excellent carriers of quantum information because they rarely interact with one another. Yet those interactions are essential for many of the calculations that quantum computers need to perform, making it difficult to build versatile machines using light alone.

Researchers from Imperial College London’s Department of Physics and collaborating institutions have developed a new approach that could help overcome this limitation. Their programmable quantum processor, called Clavina, combines different types of quantum operations in a single system, allowing it to tackle multiple computational tasks without requiring an entirely new hardware design.

The research, published in Nature Photonics, offers a promising direction for building more flexible light-based quantum computers, including systems that could eventually detect and correct their own errors.

Most photonic quantum processors are designed with a particular task in mind. Adapting them to solve another problem can require substantial changes to their hardware, limiting how easily the technology can evolve.

Clavina takes inspiration from ordinary computers, which use specialized components to handle graphics, artificial intelligence, and other demanding tasks. Instead of relying on one fixed arrangement, the new processor uses a central control unit to direct information through a programmable optical network and specialized modules.

The optical network handles linear operations, which manipulate light without requiring photons to interact. The additional modules provide nonlinear operations, expanding the kinds of calculations the system can perform. Because these components can be combined in different ways, researchers can change the processor’s functions without rebuilding it from scratch.

Dr. Shang Yu, the study’s lead author and a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellow at Imperial, said, “We set out to build a photonic quantum processor that provides a step change in functionality over our previous designs. Our new architecture ‘Clavina’ is scalable, modular and extensible, allowing different functional modules to be used depending on the computational task we wish to perform.”

To test what this flexibility could achieve, the researchers put Clavina to work on two very different challenges.

The first involved simulating the Bose-Hubbard model, a well-known problem in condensed matter physics that describes how quantum particles interact. These calculations involve many-body interactions, where the behavior of multiple particles must be considered together. Such simulations are challenging even for other quantum computing technologies, including superconducting quantum computers.

Dr. Jinzhao Sun of Queen Mary University of London explained, “The versatility of our hardware enables us to integrate nonlinear operations and linear operations. We use these operations to perform simulations involving many-body interactions, which are also restricted on superconducting quantum computers.”

The second demonstration addressed another major challenge facing quantum computing: keeping delicate quantum information safe from errors.

Quantum systems are vulnerable to noise and disturbances that can interfere with calculations. One possible solution involves creating specially structured quantum states that encode information in ways that make errors easier to detect and correct.

Among the most promising are Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states. Producing these states has been difficult for light-based systems because earlier approaches worked probabilistically, meaning researchers could not reliably generate the required states whenever they needed them.

Using Clavina, the team demonstrated a much more consistent method of generating GKP states. Although this does not mean they have built a fully error-correcting quantum computer, it addresses an important obstacle to making error correction practical.

Dr. Raj Patel, a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow who leads Imperial’s photonic quantum computing program, said, “Our architecture allows the generation of exotic quantum states such as Schrödinger cat states and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, which are valuable resources for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The nonlinear operations in our architecture provide a universal gate set at the physical level which is required for the future implementation of bosonic error-correcting codes.”

A universal gate set provides the fundamental operations that can be combined to carry out different quantum computations. Having these capabilities available in one programmable processor could support future error-correction techniques that use specially encoded states of light.

The architecture also offers possibilities beyond the two demonstrations. By allowing researchers to change or introduce functional modules, Clavina could be adapted to different scientific problems as quantum computing systems become larger and more complex.

Co-author Ying Dong of China Jiliang University said, “Previously, researchers would have to build photonic hardware tailored to a specific task. The ability to switch in different functional modules in our architecture enables a single set of hardware to perform multiple functions without overhauling the design. Clavina can solve graph problems, simulate quantum systems or generate large entangled states and resource states for error correction.”

Rather than developing a separate photonic processor for every new challenge, researchers could eventually build on the same adaptable foundation. Clavina’s demonstrations suggest that the ability to change what a quantum computer does may become just as valuable as increasing its computational power.

Reference: “Extensible universal photonic quantum computing with nonlinearity” by Shang Yu, Jinzhao Sun, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Zhi-Huai Yang, Zhenghao Li, Ewan Mer, Yazeed K. Alwehaibi, Shana H. Winston, Dayne Marcus Lopena, Zi-Cheng Zhang, Guang Yang, Runxia Tao, Mingti Zhou, Gerard J. Machado, Ying Dong, Roberto Bondesan, Vlatko Vedral, M. S. Kim, Ian A. Walmsley and Raj B. Patel, 31 July 2026, Nature Photonics. DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01962-8

#6413. From Work Mode to Wind-Down: The Benefits of Programming a Connected Home

How a tech content creator uses Hubspace from The Home Depot to streamline the smart devices that power his everyday.

A tech and lifestyle content creator by trade, Gyasi Linje looks to the latest gadgets to make his days more efficient. He relies on Hubspace from The Home Depot to control many of the smart devices in his home in one convenient place.

Hubspace, The Home Depot’s exclusive smart home platform, powers more than 250 products across select private brands—like Hampton Bay, Husky, and Vissani—as well as national brand partners. It effortlessly connects everyday essentials, including smart security, indoor and outdoor lighting, appliances, switches, watering controls, and more.

At Linje’s desk, his computer screen and speakers are plugged into a smart surge protector. He uses the app to program the lights and ceiling fan in his home office and the lock on his front door. And the presets allow Linje to work without distraction all day. “I’ve got a work-mode lighting preset,” he says. “Even my fan and dehumidifier run on a schedule.”

When the workday is over, Linje can typically either be found gaming or entertaining friends at home. Using the app, Linje can shift his living room into a colorful atmosphere for play, or into low, golden lighting that makes guests feel at ease. Plus, he can switch his freezer to fridge mode to make room for extra drinks. Hubspace even lets him know when the switch is complete, so he can time it to his guests’ arrival.

Hubspace is free to download. Once you’ve synced your home’s smart devices to the app, you can enable voice control for screen-free commands. The Hubspace app runs on WiFi and Bluetooth, so even if the WiFi is down, you can still program your home smoothly. And if you work remotely as Linje does, you can use it to set your smart devices on an automatic schedule, to help you shift in and out of your WFH routine with ease.

Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA's Voyager 1 probe will pass the one light-day mark on Nov. 18, a symbolic milestone for the agency's longest-running mission. Scientists reflect on the Voyager program's legacy and what comes next.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit, takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds.

"Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. "Not only is their data relevant, but they themselves are still out there, moving into the unknown."

Here is what the Voyagers have revealed about the solar system and interstellar space, what happens when their power finally runs out, and whether anyone — or anything — might ever intercept the messages from Earth they carry.

A NASA simulation showing where Voyager 1 is relative to the sun and solar system planets.

Voyager 1, cruising through space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), is just shy of 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) from Earth. That's the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day. The spacecraft will reach this milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. ET, after traveling through space for 49 years, two months and 11 days.

As long as that sounds, "it's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," Lee told Live Science.

If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still.

Scientifically speaking, Voyager 1 hasn't even left its home neighborhood yet. In 2012, the probe traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from incoming cosmic radiation. But it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp, which extends past the Oort Cloud — a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need about 300 more years just to reach the cloud's inner edge, and possibly 30,000 years to fly beyond it, according to NASA.

"If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still," Lee said.

On its current path, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a dim star called Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than to our own sun. Farther out, the nearest star system to our own, Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.24 light-years away — more than 1,500 times farther than Voyager 1 will be on Nov. 18.

Meanwhile Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, took a different route through the solar system after both probes launched in 1977, in order to swing past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently in interstellar space about 13 billion miles (21 million km) from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA.

An illustration of the Voyager probes passing beyond the heliopause, into interstellar space.

Crossing the one-light-day mark doesn't change how NASA communicates with the probe, though it does demand more patience.

NASA talks to the spacecraft using radio signals, which travel at the speed of light. At a distance of one light-day, a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and a reply takes another 24 hours to make the return journey.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a recent statement.

As the spacecraft continues to cruise deeper into space, that wait will grow longer. Moreover, 50 years of traversing the solar system and the increasing distance from our sun takes a toll on the probe itself. Because sunlight in the outer reaches is far too faint for solar panels, Voyager 1 relies on nuclear batteries that convert heat from the natural decay of plutonium into electricity. That supply is gradually dwindling, prompting NASA to gradually shut down nonessential instruments to conserve what energy remains and extend the mission as much as possible.

Kelly Perry, a data systems engineer on the Voyager program at JPL, told Live Science via email that the mission team's priority remains the same: "keep the spacecraft going as long as possible."

A montage of planets imaged by the twin Voyager probes, showing Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Before the Voyagers launched, the outer solar system was largely a blur of telescopic speculation. The twin probes took advantage of a planetary alignment that comes around only once every 176 years, using the gravity of giant planets to slingshot themselves onward.

Together, they have discovered 23 moons across the outer solar system, revealed faint rings around Jupiter and captured the first detailed atmospheric profiles of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They also gave the first detailed, close-up views of Jupiter's moon Europa, transforming our perception of it from a blurry speck into a remarkably smooth, geologically young world — and now one of the prime candidates for finding extraterrestrial life.

We had no idea what they looked like. And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places.

Among the more striking finds, Voyager 1 spotted active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io in 1979, the first time they had been seen on any world other than Earth.

"We had no idea what they looked like," Lee said. "And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places," he added.

"That's what Voyager was for me — a voyage of discovery," he said.

These discoveries laid the groundwork for decades of follow-up exploration, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. Decades later, as the only spacecraft to return in situ data from outside the heliosphere, the probes also proved that interstellar space is a dynamic, complex frontier rather than an empty vacuum.

Each Voyager spacecraft launched with 10 science instruments. Today, only two remain active on Voyager 1 and three on Voyager 2, measuring the magnetic fields, plasma and cosmic rays of interstellar space.

NASA began switching off the others one by one decades ago to conserve power, including the camera on Voyager 1 just minutes after it snapped the famous "Pale Blue Dot" portrait of the solar system in 1990. Ongoing power-saving reconfigurations have since helped keep the aging spacecraft operational nearly 50 years into its lifetime.

Voyager's iconic "Pale Blue Dot" image shows Earth as a "mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam," in the words of Carl Sagan.

In one such recent effort, nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers shut off certain high-power subsystems while switching on lower-power alternatives, which "bought us almost two more years during which we will not need to turn any instrument off," Perry said.

With onboard power steadily dwindling, however, "there's a recognition that it won't be forever," Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at the Grand Valley State University in Michigan who co-authored an upcoming book about the Golden Record aboard the Voyager probes, told Live Science.

Because Voyager is a science mission, its mission will be considered finished when "no science instruments are operational," Perry said. "The Science Team decided that the last remaining instrument will be the magnetometer," she added. "We will never intentionally power off this instrument."

After the science data eventually stops, both probes may still keep beaming back basic engineering updates, such as about their health and power status, until around 2036, according to NASA. Even after the spacecraft finally fall silent, they will keep coasting through interstellar space, and "analysis shows that they should remain intact," Perry said.

Scientists will still be able to calculate their positions based on their last known speed and trajectories, Weibel said. "We'll know intellectually where it is unless it gets intercepted."

An illustration of Voyager shown next to the Golden Record.

Theoretically, yes. But interstellar space is so unfathomably vast that the chances of aliens finding the probes are vanishingly small, Lee said.

That makes it unlikely that aliens will ever find the Voyager Golden Records — twin gold-plated discs meant to portray the diversity of life on Earth. They hold sounds such as wind and animal calls, greetings in 55 languages, images of our planet and a celestial map pinpointing its location — all intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and playing them. (The probes also carry visual instructions for spinning the records).

In that sense, the Golden Records are as much an artistic exercise as a scientific one.

"The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian — not that it's likely — are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, and then playing the record," Lee said.

Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort

If an extraterrestrial civilization did find the probe after we lost contact with it, "we would have no way of knowing," Weibel added. "It becomes something that's powered entirely by imagination at that point."

So why send a message at all? All three scientists interviewed for this story see the Golden Record as a cosmic time capsule, a symbolic gesture meant to unite humanity around a shared home planet. For all its imperfections, including the omission of some widely spoken languages and a few mislabeled tracks, the disc remains an enduring emblem of human presence on Earth, they said.

"Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," Perry told Live Science. "Although I won't be able to speak to the Voyager spacecraft any more, I love knowing that I'll always be able to look to the stars and know they're still on their way."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. #6410. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.

#6406. What happened when scientists kept birds and bats away from cocoa trees?

An experiment on cocoa farms in the Peruvian Amazon reveals how nearby trees, birds, and bats can help protect the harvest.

In the Peruvian Amazon, the trees beyond a cocoa farm can help determine how much cocoa it produces.

Farms surrounded by forests, orchards, and other tree crops had some of the highest yields in a new study, and an experiment pointed to an unlikely pair of allies: birds and bats.

To find out how much those animals mattered, researchers put nets around some cocoa trees and left others open.

Where forests covered 30–35% of the surrounding landscape, the cocoa trees that birds and bats could reach produced nearly twice as much as the netted trees.

An international team led by the University of Vienna mapped the connections between shade trees, wildlife, and cocoa productivity across 28 organic agroforests in the northern Peruvian Amazon.

The researchers estimated that cocoa trees accessible to birds and bats would yield about 265 kilograms per hectare per year where trees covered roughly 20% of the surrounding landscape.

Where surrounding tree cover reached 70–80%, the estimated yield was nearly four times as high, at about 1,000 kilograms per hectare per year.

At 2023 cocoa prices, the researchers valued the extra cocoa associated with bird and bat activity at about US$1,640 per hectare per year.

For smallholder farmers in a region where average incomes are modest, that’s not a rounding error. It’s the difference between scraping by and building something.

“Birds and bats can be powerful allies for cacao farmers, but only if the surrounding landscape provides enough habitat. If these landscapes become large monocultures, much of this natural pest-control benefit is lost,” said senior author Bea Maas from the University of Vienna.

The intuitive assumption – more shade trees, more biodiversity, better farm – doesn’t hold up cleanly.

Shade-tree cover benefitted wildlife, improved soils, and buffered temperature extremes. But very dense shade starved the cocoa of light and substantially cut yields.

On farms in tree-rich landscapes, a mix of tall and short shade trees helped support biodiversity.

Dense shade, meanwhile, reduced cocoa yields by limiting sunlight.

“Our data show that cacao farms do not need uniform shade to support biodiversity. A mosaic of tall and short trees, tree clusters and open patches can create habitat for wildlife while maintaining production,” said lead author Aycart-Lazo from the University of Vienna.

The researchers surveyed birds, bats, and arthropods. They measured cocoa yield, natural pest control, pollination rates, pest and disease incidence, soil fertility, and microclimate.

Then they used drone imagery and remote-sensing data to connect what was happening inside each farm to what the surrounding landscape looked like.

The finding that probably matters most for policy is this: what’s outside the farm fence may be more important than what’s inside it.

A farmer can do everything right on their own plot and still lose most of the pest-control benefit if the surrounding land has been stripped bare.

This is an uncomfortable truth for programs that focus exclusively on farm-level certification.

A certified organic plot in a deforested landscape doesn’t get the same ecosystem services as one embedded in a matrix of forests and orchards.

“Our results show that these benefits depend strongly on how trees are managed both within farms and across the surrounding landscape,” Aycart-Lazo said.

The team proposes a landscape-level formula for the region: roughly 30–35% forest cover, another 40–45% in tree-based habitats like agroforests or orchards, and 20–30% in open areas for annual crops.

That mix, they argue, could create multifunctional landscapes that sustain both high biodiversity and strong cocoa production.

This is a recommendation though, not a decree. Different regions have different land pressures, different communities, and different histories.

“This is not a one-size-fits-all blueprint. Landscape strategies need to be adapted to local land availability and developed together with local communities,” Ocampo-Ariza said.

The study was conducted in one of the world’s most biodiverse regions. The specifics belong to the northern Peruvian Amazon.

But the underlying logic is portable. Wherever crops depend on natural pest control, the surrounding habitat either supports or undermines it.

The study cuts against a stubborn narrative in tropical agriculture – that farmers must choose between productivity and conservation. The data from these 28 Peruvian farms suggest the opposite.

Biodiversity didn’t just coexist with cocoa production. It actively drove it.

The ecosystem services provided by wildlife – pest control above all – were the mechanism converting habitat into yield.

That doesn’t mean conservation is free. Managing a structurally varied canopy takes skill.

Maintaining landscape-level forest cover requires coordination across farms, communities, and governments. But the economic argument is now harder to wave away.

For cocoa growers, keeping forests nearby can help protect the harvest.

The study is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6405. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

K.L. Wahlstrom et al. Direct electrical stimulation of the human amygdala enhances recognition memory for objects but not scenes. Communications Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s42003-026-10270-4

#6404. One November storm changed how California’s Sierra Nevada looked from orbit

An early storm brought nearly a foot of snow to Donner Pass, offering a first look at the snowpack that helps supply California with water.

Fresh snow stretches across California’s Sierra Nevada in a satellite image taken on the morning of November 14.

Around Lake Tahoe and farther south, white covers much of the high country.

Along part of the range’s western side, green slopes still show through, making it easy to see where the storm left its mark.

A Pacific storm swept through the previous day, bringing heavy rain to the Sacramento area and close to a foot of snow to some mountain locations.

A break between weather systems gave NASA’s Terra satellite a clear look at the mountains after one of the season’s first major snowfalls.

The instrument that captured the view, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, or MODIS, takes in long stretches of the mountain range at once.

From that vantage point, the snow that fell on individual peaks and mountain passes comes into view as a broad band of white.

NASA Earth Observatory paired the November 14 view with an image from two days earlier, when snow was largely confined to the highest ridges southeast of Lake Tahoe.

The earlier view gives a sense of how much changed in the time it took for one storm to cross California.

A separate regional analysis from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated that snow covered about 43 percent of its Sierra Nevada analysis area on November 14.

A month earlier, the estimate was less than 1 percent. The comparison shows how quickly snow can spread across terrain that was largely bare in mid-October.

At Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory recorded nearly 12 inches of snow on November 13.

Officials closed Interstate 80 in both directions over Donner Summit that evening.

Farther south, Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches of fresh snow. In Yosemite National Park, officials closed several roads ahead of the storm.

The reports from Donner Pass and Mammoth give a sense of how much snow fell at specific locations across the long stretch of mountains visible from above.

The storm also brought heavy rain to the Sacramento area, west of the Sierra Nevada.

Elevation helped determine what reached the ground. Where the air was warm enough, precipitation fell as rain.

Higher in the mountains, colder conditions allowed snow to accumulate.

The green slopes along the western side of the range are a reminder that a storm can bring very different weather to places only a short distance apart.

The broad cover visible on November 14 raises a question that matters well beyond the mountains.

How much water is in all that snow? Hydrologists answer it by measuring snow water equivalent, the depth of water that would remain if the snow at a given spot melted.

A foot of light, powdery snow can hold less water than a shallower layer of dense, wet snow.

California’s Department of Water Resources uses that measurement to help forecast how much water could flow out of the mountains as the snow melts.

Some of that runoff reaches major reservoirs in spring and early summer, helping supply water during the state’s dry months.

Timing matters because California receives much of its precipitation during the cooler part of the year.

Rain can reach streams and reservoirs soon after a storm.

Snow can stay in the mountains for months before melting, releasing some of that water later, when storms are less frequent.

The November storm arrived about six weeks into the water year, the 12-month period hydrologists use to track precipitation and runoff beginning October 1.

The Sierra Nevada snowpack generally peaks around April 1, leaving several months for new storms to add to it or for warm spells to melt some of what has already accumulated.

More snow was already in the forecast when NASA released the image on November 18.

The National Weather Service had issued a winter storm warning for parts of the Sierra Nevada through November 20, with around four feet of snow possible at some locations above 8,000 feet.

The November 14 image captures the mountains at the start of that longer process.

In a single day, snow spread across enough of the Sierra Nevada to change how the range looked from orbit.

Over the coming months, the same slopes will collect or lose snow with each shift in the weather.

By spring, what remains will help determine how much meltwater reaches California’s reservoirs as the state heads into its dry season.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

Since becoming a freelancer, Victoria has expanded her focus to explore topics from across the sciences and has also worked with Chemistry Review, Neon Squid Publishing and the Open University, amongst others. #6401. Office light may throw off the body’s daily rhythm

In a study of day-active rats, an hour of simulated daylight at noon helped restore activity rhythms weakened by fluorescent office lighting.

People spend about 90% of their time indoors, under ceiling lights that are a small fraction as bright as the sky outside. The body reads that light as a biological signal.

In a rodent that keeps human hours, living under standard fluorescent office light weakened the animal’s daily rhythm of activity.

An hour of simulated daylight at noon each day, roughly analogous to a lunchtime walk outdoors, partly restored the rats’ daily activity rhythm.

In a second experiment, more of the male rats that spent six weeks under fluorescent light showed diabetic-range blood sugar than rats under daylight-strength light.

A smaller share of sperm were moving in the fluorescent-light group, about 19% compared with 45% under simulated daylight.

The study is small, with eight animals in the first experiment and 20 in the second, and all of them were male.

Lily Yan, a professor in the Department of Psychology at Michigan State University, led the work. The lead author is Antony Bum Kim of the Department of Architecture at the University of California, Berkeley.

“It is a biological signal that influences circadian organization and, potentially, a range of downstream health outcomes,” Yan said of light.

The body’s internal clock helps regulate daily patterns, known as circadian rhythms, in sleep, appetite, and much else.

Nearly every lab rodent is awake at night, which makes it a poor stand-in for a person whose body clock runs on daylight.

The Nile grass rat, a small African rodent, is active in the daytime, and Yan’s lab has used it for years to study how light affects the brain.

Over each cage, the team installed a programmable light that can imitate the color mix of many sources. Its daylight setting ran at about 5,600 lux, roughly the level that building designers treat as true daylight.

The office setting imitated a standard fluorescent tube at about 150 lux, the brightness of a typical indoor workspace.

Eight male grass rats lived under four lighting schedules in turn, two weeks each. Sensors logged their movement day and night.

The first schedule was steady daylight from dawn to dusk. The second was daylight that brightened to the same midday peak and faded again, which delivered about half the total light.

The third was fluorescent office light all day. The fourth was office light with one hour of full daylight at noon.

The rats were most active, and most sharply divided between a busy day and a quiet night, under steady daylight.

Under fluorescent light their activity was lower and their rhythm flatter, with its peak shifted later in the day.

The ramped daylight did not match the steady version even though it reached the same peak.

The authors wrote that the total amount of light over the day, more than its brightest moment, seems to set the strength of the rhythm.

Adding the noon hour of daylight to the office schedule raised the strength of the rhythm again, though only partly.

All eight animals showed a burst of activity during that hour. The authors called it a partial rescue.

A separate group of 20 male grass rats lived for six weeks under either steady daylight or fluorescent light, 10 in each group.

The rats’ body weight, belly fat, and average blood sugar did not differ between the groups.

But five of the 20 animals had blood sugar in a range the lab treats as diabetic, and four of the five had lived under fluorescent light.

In a follow-up with a different way of drawing blood, the pattern held. Four of eight rats under fluorescent light crossed that line, compared with one of seven under daylight.

The two groups produced the same number of sperm. Under daylight, about 45% of those sperm were moving. Under fluorescent light, about 19% were.

“Factors affecting health are not limited to drugs, diet and exercise,” Kim said. “The light environments we create in our homes, schools and workplaces are also biological exposures.”

Ten animals per group is a small sample. More rats under fluorescent light crossed the study’s threshold for diabetic-range blood sugar, while average blood sugar was similar in the two groups.

The authors also wrote that blood drawn after euthanasia can read differently, which is why they ran the follow-up.

Every animal was male, so the study says nothing about females. And a grass rat under a programmable lamp is not an office worker with windows, a commute, and a phone.

The authors wrote that the findings support daylight deficiency as a risk factor for diabetes in this animal.

The sperm result is new, they wrote, since earlier work on light and sperm looked at day length rather than light quality.

What remains untested is whether the same shifts happen in people. The authors wrote that the next step is for other groups to repeat the work in grass rats or other day-active animals.

The next question is whether an hour of brighter light at midday could help people who work far from a window maintain a stronger daily rhythm.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Biological Rhythms.

#6400. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6399. The fight to save one of Australia’s rarest frogs has taken a cue from farmers

Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.

A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.

Researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus. That means selective breeding could make the species more resilient.

The frog is functionally extinct in the wild. The culprit is chytridiomycosis, an infectious disease caused by the amphibian chytrid fungus.

Captive breeding has kept the species alive. But returning frogs to the wild is hard because the fungus persists in the environment.

Lead author Mikaeylah Davidson completed the work as part of her PhD at the University of Melbourne.

The study tested whether genomic selection could guide conservation breeding for the frog.

Davidson and her colleagues combined laboratory experiments with genome-wide genetic information. That included a custom genotyping array built for the frog.

The team found that southern corroboree frogs differ in how long they survive after exposure to chytrid fungus. Some of that variation is inherited.

“Using genomic data, we were able to show that survival following chytrid infection is a heritable trait, meaning some of the differences in survival are due to genetic differences that can be passed on to the next generation,” Davidson said.

“This means there is genetic variation we could potentially use to improve survival through selective breeding.”

“Excitingly, this approach is a potential way to move beyond simply keeping endangered frogs alive in captivity, towards actively improving their ability to cope with the threats preventing their recovery in the wild.”

Modeling suggested genomic information could guide breeding decisions.

It could potentially increase average survival time after exposure to chytrid fungus by around nine percent in the next generation.

The model projected that gain while accounting for inbreeding and genetic diversity.

An established captive breeding program offered a chance to test the idea in practice. Zoos Victoria and the Taronga Conservation Society support that program through partnerships.

The research suggests improved disease resilience doesn’t need to come at the expense of genetic diversity. That is especially significant for small, critically endangered populations.

In such groups, maintaining diversity and limiting inbreeding are central to long-term population health and evolutionary potential.

Senior author Lee Skerratt from the University of Melbourne argued the approach may also have potential for other threatened wildlife affected by persistent disease.

That is particularly true for species already managed through captive breeding.

“Amphibians are an important focus, with hundreds of species now maintained in captivity for conservation as chytrid fungus continues to threaten populations globally,” he said.

“Genomic selection could help conservation breeding programs move beyond preventing extinction by moving animals into captivity towards actively supporting animals’ ability to survive threats in the wild.”

First, researchers developed the genomic tools and disease datasets needed to explore new strategies for the frog. They then combined a newly mapped genome and a custom genotyping array with extensive disease-resilience data.

That let them investigate selective breeding as a proactive approach to species recovery.

The next stage is to improve and validate the predictions.

The team will use genomic information from more of the breeding population. They will also explore other genetic approaches to improve disease resistance.

Researchers will also test whether the predicted improvements show up in later generations. And critically, they will check whether greater survival in the lab translates into better outcomes in the wild.

Amphibians are in deep trouble worldwide. The chytrid fungus has caused catastrophic declines and extinctions.

More than 200 threatened frog species are now kept in captivity. These colonies have prevented immediate extinctions.

But they are temporary refuges, meant to hold the line until threats can be mitigated.

Selective breeding offers a different path. Instead of just keeping animals alive, it can improve their ability to cope. That could raise the odds of successful reintroduction.

While genomic selection has transformed plant and animal breeding, it has rarely been applied to wildlife. The main barriers have been missing datasets and a lack of structured breeding programs.

This frog had both, which made it an ideal test case.

The species produces fewer than 30 eggs per year and reaches sexual maturity at 2 to 5 years of age. Those traits slow generational turnover.

The trait is also polygenic. No single gene has a large effect. Resistance is shaped by many loci, each contributing a little.

Because many genes contribute to survival, the team used genomic selection, which draws on information from across the genome.

And the modelling covers only part of the breeding population. Future work could capture more genetic variation.

First, refine the breeding value predictions with more parental genotyping. Second, test realized responses in controlled and semi-natural conditions. Third, run multi-generational selective breeding alongside ongoing diversity management.

Data from each phase would feed back into the program. That supports adaptive management and continuous improvement.

For now, the result is a proof of concept. It shows that captive populations can become more than passive safeguards. For a frog on the brink, that shift could matter a great deal.

The study is published in the journal npj Biodiversity.

Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

#6395. The power grid’s toughest hour of the year may no longer come on a summer afternoon

Heat pumps could reshape the power grid more than climate change, pushing the worst demand spikes in cold regions into winter by 2060.

Ask when the power grid has its hardest day and most people picture a heat wave, with every air conditioner in town running at once.

Across much of the northern United States, that day may soon be a cold winter night instead.

New modeling finds that as homes swap gas furnaces for heat pumps, the worst spikes in electricity demand in cold regions could grow by half to nearly double by 2060.

With today’s heating and cooling equipment, warming alone changes extreme peaks by less than 10% in either direction.

The model projects much larger increases in cold regions as buildings switch to electric heating.

Mai Shi, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Michigan‘s School for Environment and Sustainability, led the work with colleagues at Michigan, MIT and Cornell University.

Their projections cover 183 counties through 2060 and hold the number of buildings fixed. Every change they report comes from weather and equipment, not from new construction or population growth.

“We focused on the extreme peak demands because we want to keep our power systems reliable,” Shi said.

“If the system works for moderate conditions but fails in extremes, it doesn’t work. That’s not how we build the power grid. We need to plan for extremes.”

An electric heat pump can both heat and cool a building. When it replaces a gas furnace, heating shifts onto the power grid. The standard heat pump in the study lost heating capacity as outdoor temperatures fell.

The standard unit in the study keeps only half of its rated heating capacity at 5°F (-15°C).

In the team’s model, heat pumps and insulation spread through buildings at the pace home air conditioning spread across the country, about 10% a year.

With that pace of adoption and today’s weather, the most extreme peaks grow by 60% to 104% by 2060 across the six cold regions.

Those are New England, New York, the Midwest, the Mid-Atlantic, the Northwest and the Great Plains. The season changes too.

At the start of the projections, more than 95% of those regions’ yearly peaks fall in summer.

By 2060, more than 95% fall in winter. Insulation lowers demand, but in cold regions it can’t cancel out the furnaces being replaced.

Run the same buildings through a warming climate with today’s equipment and the changes are smaller.

Extreme peaks rise 3% to 9% in every region but the Northwest, as extreme heat pushes up cooling demand. In the Northwest, winter heating already sets the peak, and a milder winter trims it by 3%.

Put the two drivers together and they don’t simply add up. Warmer winters offset part of the heat pump demand, cutting the growth in cold-region extremes by up to 18% compared with technology alone.

The net result in those regions is still a 48% to 93% increase through 2060. That is up to roughly 10 times what warming alone would do. Warming also delays the switch to winter peaking rather than stopping it.

Researchers call the spread of a technology through homes tech diffusion.

“Tech diffusion may have a larger impact than climate change on peak demand in a lot of regions,” said Shi, who is also a member of the university’s Center for Sustainable Systems.

In the projections for California and Texas, the peak stays in summer. Heat pumps and insulation make cooling more efficient there, so the technology lowers extreme peaks instead of raising them.

With warming included, those two regions’ extremes end up 1% to 9% lower than they would be under climate change alone.

The Southwest and Southeast are in between. Technology alone pushes their extremes up 17% and 11%, because about 60% of their yearly peaks move to winter while the rest stay in summer.

A winter peak on a cold night can run higher than a summer one. Warming lowers those winter extremes by 4% to 6%.

In Texas, faster adoption lowers the peak further. Under climate change alone, the largest peak between 2020 and 2060 is 12% above today’s.

With the fastest spread of heat pumps and insulation, that increase shrinks to 5%.

The team trained 209,352 machine learning models on simulated hourly heating and cooling use for 362,227 homes and commercial buildings across 183 counties.

The counties were chosen so that each state’s mix of weather zones matched the real one.

The researchers used 100 simulations from four climate models and three emissions scenarios to project how future weather could affect electricity demand for heating and cooling.

Adoption speed came from history. The researchers looked at how fast 18 past technologies spread, from vacuum cleaners at about 2% a year to cell phones at about 36%. Home air conditioning, at 10%, was their main case.

The researchers used the 95th percentile of projected annual peaks to estimate extreme demand. Only about one in 20 of those peaks exceeds that level.

In the projections, peaks change little through the early 2030s and the weather is nearly the whole source of uncertainty. In cold regions, that changes in the late 2030s and the 2040s.

Heat pump adoption reaches the steep part of its curve and winter peaks grow quickly. From one climate run to the next, it becomes uncertain whether a year’s peak falls in summer or winter.

The spread of possible peaks in those regions widens to three or four times its 2020 level by the 2050s. By then, winter peaking is established in most of them.

For grid planners, the source of uncertainty moves with that transition. By the 2050s, how fast people adopt the technology is the largest single factor in New England and New York, at 65% to 75% of the total.

Climate still drives 85% to 99% in the Southeast, the Northwest and California.

Michael Craig is the study’s senior author and an associate professor at Michigan.

“Climate change still matters a lot. If I’m thinking about my power system and what I should worry about, climate change is still an important source of risk and uncertainty,” Craig said.

The team also tested a heat pump that keeps 90% of its heating capacity at 5°F instead of 50%. With it, extreme peaks come out 5% to 40% lower, with the biggest savings in cold regions.

The projections hold the equipment’s performance fixed over 40 years, so they don’t include heat pumps improving, or smart thermostats and thermal storage moving demand off the worst hours. They cover heating and cooling only.

Electric vehicle charging isn’t in them, and neither are data centers.

One recent tally of utility forecasts attributes roughly half of the projected growth in U.S. peak load through 2030 to data centers.

Humidity isn’t in the model either, only temperature. And it assumes heat pumps spread at the same pace everywhere, when energy prices, housing and policy will set different speeds in different states.

How fast adoption will actually run in each region is the open question. Shi said that number, unlike the weather, is one that local rules and incentives can steer.

The authors wrote that the next step is building those regional differences into the projections, so that each region’s planners see the projection that applies to them.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
