#6354. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Disease outbreaks revealed a weakened federal response

Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and New York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy says.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she said they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”

When the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli says.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” says Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the New York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm says. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a new one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

Pandora is the trending news editor at Live Science. She is also a science presenter and previously worked as Senior Science and Health Reporter at Newsweek. Pandora holds a Biological Sciences degree from the University of Oxford, where she specialised in biochemistry and molecular biology.

#6352. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column

Thursday, November 19Sunrise: 6:50 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 1:41 P.M.Moonset: 1:07 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:29 P.M.Moonset: 3:22 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%)

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:59 P.M.Moonset: 4:34 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%)

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus, also in Taurus, at 2 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 4:24 P.M.Moonset: 7:10 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%)

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 5:24 P.M.Moonset: 8:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%)

Thursday, November 26Sunrise: 6:58 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 6:35 P.M.Moonset: 9:33 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%)

Friday, November 27Sunrise: 6:59 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 7:53 P.M.Moonset: 10:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6351. Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A star called “Little Bao” danced with its giant partner “Big Bao”

An image captured by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) telescope shows the Andromeda galaxy, which is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way — and the home galaxy of Big and Little Bao.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

#6350. Nov. 19, 1969: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon

Five days after their Nov. 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms). Part of Apollo 12’s mission was to demonstrate improvements to the precision of lunar landings, and Conrad piloted the Intrepid Lunar Module to a pinpoint landing on Nov. 19. While their crewmate Richard Gordon remained in the Command Module (Yankee Clipper) above them, Conrad and Bean began the first of their two moonwalks. Conrad descended the ladder from the LM first, and as he stepped onto the Moon quipped, “Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that’s a long one for me.”

Although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful. The astronauts collected rock and soil samples and deployed their Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package (ALSEP), which included a solar wind collector, and seismometer, and a magnetometer. They also visited the Surveyor 3 unmanned lander (which had been on the Moon since 1967), retrieving several components of the spacecraft to return to Earth for study. After 31 and a half hours on the Moon, nearly eight hours of those spent in EVAs, Intrepid lifted off and re-docked with Yankee Clipper. The crew safely splashed down back on Earth on Nov. 24.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

#6348. Are US Flight Schedules Returning to Normal? What Thanksgiving Travelers Need to Know

Travel chaos erupted at US airports over the weekend following a historic FAA ground stop that paused all flight takeoffs across the country for nearly five hours.

The ground stop, declared by the FAA amid air traffic control issues on Friday, November 13, stranded millions of fliers nationwide, with tens of thousands of flight delays and cancellations continuing for days. Now, with the busy Thanksgiving travel period fast approaching, travelers are wondering when US air travel system will return to normal.

Fortunately for travelers, both federal officials and airlines are doing everything they can to get flight schedules back on track and have airport operations running smoothly in time for the holiday rush. “Recovery to normal operations will be slow and steady,” says a November 15 statement from the FAA. “We ask for your patience as airlines work to get you to your destination.”

Although the incident is frustrating, experts say that travelers shouldn’t be concerned about the safety of the air traffic control system. “While the disruption was significant, travelers should take confidence in knowing that safety remained the top priority throughout the incident,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of the US Travel Association. “Our aviation professionals deserve tremendous credit for managing the crisis and getting Americans safely back on their way."

If you have Thanksgiving travel plans and you're flying out this week, here's what to know about the current state of air travel in the US.

The ground stop was issued due to air traffic control equipment outages and issues with telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” says the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”

On Friday afternoon, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The company was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” says an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”

Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA says that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications issues are still under investigation.

Regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a Sunday interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”

Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Freeman. “Friday's disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”

Air travel experts say that the ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans beginning later this week should be minimal.

As of Monday afternoon, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. There were still about 2,800 flight delays within, into, or out of the US on Monday, and nearly 330 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware data. It also helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this year compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually the busiest air travel day of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying,

American Airlines, the largest carrier at DFW, said its operations were returning to normal on Monday. “American is prepared to operate a largely normal schedule Monday, Nov. 16, following the FAA's nationwide ground stop,” the carrier said in a statement. "With crews and aircraft in position and favorable weather expected across our system, we are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event.”

Delta has also advised its passengers traveling on Monday to continue to allow extra time at the airport for any lingering effects on flight schedules. “While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations,” the carrier said.

Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop. However, two major carriers still have travel waivers in place.

Delta is still allowing passengers scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16, to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Travelers’ new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

American Airlines is waiving change fees for passengers booked to travel to or from one of 21 major US airports through Wednesday, November 18. Passengers can choose a new travel date through November 21, but all changes must be made by November 18.

Even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

It’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages over the long run.

“The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”

Airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6346. Hear stars being born in Chandra’s new sonifications

Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center launched A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

Our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound

On November 17, Chandra released four new sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

Each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

At around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

About 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and shows up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with new instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

Some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode quickly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

The Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s new album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123

#6344. Well-Traveled Women on Where They Plan to Visit in 2027

A bucket list item is one thing—turning it into an itinerary is another. The difference often lies in deciding that the places we dream about are worth pursuing amid limited vacation days and financial constraints. It’s a sentiment captured by avid traveler and content creator, Lucrenzia Worthington: “If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.”

With 2027 in sight, we’re taking inspiration from well-traveled women who are already thinking about the possibilities of the fresh, new year ahead and the trips they hope to pull off. Spanning photographers, artisans, interior designers, rock climbers, divers, and cookbook authors, their wanderlust is as varied as it is far-reaching. Read on for how they plan to travel next, from diving Antarctica’s crystalline waters to cooking in the fertile valleys of the Peloponnese Peninsula.

“For as long as I can remember, I’ve dreamed of diving in Antarctica. Maybe it’s growing up in Bangkok’s tropical heat, but the polar regions endlessly fascinate me: the icebergs, the seals, and penguins. I’ve visited the White Continent before, but seeing it underwater is something else entirely. In 2027, I’m joining Aurora Expeditions, a pioneer in polar diving for over 20 years. Even as an experienced diver and underwater photographer, it takes serious preparation: I’m logging drysuit dives off [the coast of] Cape Town with specialized gear to get ready for one of the most extraordinary dive sites on earth.” —Pier Nirandara, travel writer, underwater photographer, and founder of Immersiv Expeditions

“You know, I've been lucky enough to see some extraordinary corners of the world, yet one place keeps slipping down my list. It's always ’not the right time,’ always ’too complicated to book.’ But 2027 is the year: Lapland, in February. There are direct flights from Milan to Rovaniemi, Finland, and I would plan two nights there and two in Levi. I'm dreaming of a night in those super cool glass cabins where you fall asleep under the northern lights and endless starry skies, and booking experiences like visiting a reindeer farm, husky sledding, and snowshoe hikes through frosted pines—but also cozy up indoors by a crackling fire, with a warm blanket, and soak up the winter wonderland around me. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that it’s never the right time, only the time you finally decide to go.” —Lucrezia Worthington, content creator and freelance journalist

“I've always wanted to visit Morocco, and I think 2027 is the year. My dream is to stay in a riad in Marrakech with however many friends I can persuade to join me. I want to find tagine and wander through the [medina]. I also hope to venture out to the Atlas Mountains for a weekend.” —Ríoghnach Robinson, author of Bad Words

“In 2027, I'm planning to return to Antalya, Turkey. I spent a week there this year and fell in love with the food, the people, and the climbing. I'll be based around Geyikbayırı and Çitdibi, where there are limestone crags in the hills with views out to the sea. I usually find a place to stay on Airbnb and lean on local recommendations for where to eat. One spot I'm definitely returning to is Coffee Roaster 404.” —Sasha DiGiulian, professional climber and founder of SEND Bars

“Most flock to Greece for the idyllic beaches and all things Mediterranean, and while I completely understand that desire, my curiosity has landed me in the Peloponnese Peninsula, in particular the central region of Arcadia. Its fertile valleys are known for strong culinary and agricultural traditions; apples, sour cherries, slender eggplants, cheeses from mountain sheep and goats, walnuts, chestnuts, and mushroom foraging. I have been obsessing over a beautiful hotel that caught my eye: Manna, located on Mount Mainalo among hiking trails and dense forests. The mountain is also known for a very special high altitude honey cultivated from fir trees. Honestly, the honey alone is enough to get me on a plane.” —Noreen Wasti, cook, food creative, and author of Feast Your Eyes: Beautiful Recipes to Garnish, Share, and Savor

“In 2027, I’d love to finally visit Peru and see Machu Picchu. South America is completely new territory for me, and the landscapes, craftsmanship, and food are all calling. I’m imagining local guides, time in the Sacred Valley, and plenty of exploring. I’d also love to go home to Mauritius, but this time be a tourist. A beautiful hotel, all the food I miss, and time to enjoy the island and its lovely hospitality. Usually, my visits revolve around family and catching up. In 2027, for once, I’d like my biggest responsibility to be deciding what to have for lunch.” —Nashmita Rajiah, interior designer

“I’m perpetually scouting [destinations] for In Hand’s newsletter and group trips by exploring culturally rich regions through the lens of traditional craft. I'm looking forward to an upcoming trip to the Atlas Mountains to visit the female Amazigh weavers in their homes, and learning about the by-hand process of weaving Berber rugs at the source rather than the point of sale, focusing on the culture and traditions around this generation-to-generation craft. I’m staying at Kasbah du Toubkal in Imlil, a small mountain town grounded in real Amazigh village life. It’s a trip I’ve wanted to take for years. ” —Meghan McEwen, writer and founder of group trip planner In Hand

“What I look forward to most is traveling with friends and family. Mornings in the sea, a simple lunch in the hot sun. Afternoons are for slow wandering, and at night we'll cook big meals from our market finds. In 2027, my family is heading to Sicily for two weeks in shoulder season, before the [summer] tourist wave. The first half we'll explore the main island, from the salt flats of Trapani to the bone white cliffs of Scala dei Turchi on the south coast. Then Favignana in the Egadi Islands, off Sicily's west coast, will hopefully be home for a week or so. The water is crystal blue, the coves are plentiful, and you can bike around the entire island easily. Tuna is still king there, though the old canning factory has long since closed. I'm dreaming of spaghetti with bottarga. At the moment I have my eyes on Villa Zu Nillu from The Thinking Traveller, perched above its own labyrinthine Roman stone quarry, into which a beautiful pool and a Mediterranean garden have been set. And I will document it all.” —Andrea Gentl, photographer and author of Cooking with Mushrooms

“After last summer’s European heatwave, we’re planning a cooler 2027 Finnish escape with my decorative arts grad school friend and her family. We always mix design with fun for the kids, so we’ll visit Helsinki’s Aalto House, the design district, and Hvitträsk museum before renting a lakeside mökki for swimming, hiking, and archipelago adventures. I want to experience the “midnight sun,” but I might regret it if the kids never sleep. Truthfully, I’m more of a lazy reptile than an outdoor adventurer, so afterward, our family of four will retreat to a less popular Italian beach for pasta, sunshine, and absolutely no obligation to do anything adventurous at all.” —Ajiri Aki, author of JOIE: A Parisian’s Guide to Celebrating The Good Life and The Joie Journal

“Long the secret destination of all the chic Italians I know, the low-key vibe of Maremma [in Tuscany and Lazio] is starting to also draw an international crowd looking for relaxed summers featuring all the best of Italy—raw nature, excellent food—minus the crowds and bling. For families, the Terre di Sacra Estate is on my wish list, either “glamping” on the beach or in one of their villas. And speaking of villas, Maremma doyenne Amanda Sposito is behind one of the most beautiful private rentals, the Villa Tre Querce, in town.” —Philomena Schurer Merckoll, founder of Riad Mena and hospitality group Egypt Beyond

“I would love to visit Japan. Surprisingly, I have never been to Asia before, so it feels like a whole new world waiting to be explored. As a designer working with raffia and traditional weaving techniques, I am fascinated by Japan’s appreciation for craftsmanship and handmade objects. I would love to explore Kyoto’s historic temples, meet local artisans, and learn about their weaving traditions and use of natural materials. Seeing Mount Fuji in person would also be incredible: I find so much inspiration in the colors, textures, and everyday details of a place, and I would love to bring those experiences into my designs.” —Akosua Afriyie-Kumi, founder of AAKS

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
