#6278. At Dior’s First Spa in Venice, Old Glamour Gets the Hi-Tech Treatment

The buzz of the Venice Film Festival has only just died down, when I step out of a Riva boat that bobs at the berth of the Hotel Cipriani Venice on Giudecca Island. I’m excited but also exhausted after spending the previous ten days on several long-haul flights, and I fear it’s beginning to affect my conversational skills—and my collagen levels. Luckily, I’m not here to attend a premiere or hop between Biennale events. I'm here to experience Cipriani's newly opened Dior Spa, the fashion house's first in Venice.

Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.

The views from my suite's private terrace

A welcome Dior takeover on Cip's ground floor

Sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which launched its new spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino. The cream and pastel palette channels an 18th-century Venetian Rococo spirit, with elegant mid-century Italian stucco and terrazzo flooring. Science-driven skincare nerds tend to believe that fashion houses can’t run beauty departments worthy of their approval, but Dior has the potential to persuade them otherwise. Many luxury spas are often either visually stunning temples that offer underwhelming treatments, or medically-driven centers that leave you glowing but feeling as if you’re in a hospital. Dior combines the best of both worlds, recalling an old-school glamour while deploying higher-tech treatments that aren’t geared towards “maxxing” but aim for clients to look and feel their best in a tranquil environment.

The Dior Spa's La Collection Privée island

After spending the morning in Murano watching the world’s most talented glassblowers at work, I head down to the spa’s marbled entrance where a Murano chandelier dangles above a centerpiece table festooned with beautiful bottles of parfums from Dior’s La Collection Privée, including Tobacolore and, my favorite fragrance, La Colle Noire. I’m handed a rose infusion before slipping into cloud-soft Dior slippers and waiting outside my treatment room for one of the signature treatments, which include Le Théâtre Corporal, a four-handed, Ayurvedic-inspired massage (which couples can do together), and the Golden Aura hydrafacial. But I’m here for what feels like the most apt option in a city famed for its masked balls: the Mascarade facial.

Setting up for a canalside Dior masterclass

Developed by the brand’s global skincare ambassador, Hadda Akrim, the Mascarade aims to regenerate the skin and soothe the mind. I’m in need of it now that my circadian rhythm is disrupted after back-to-back flights, cabin pressure and changing time zones. The treatment is more than just a facial: it involves 90 minutes of drainage, rebalancing, and re-boosting with the help of devices that encourage the nutrients being massaged into your skin to sink deeper. Firstly, I lie on the treatment table to receive an abdominal massage, which rebalances my nervous system (the gut is our second brain, after all) and restores my inner harmony to maximize my radiance.

Next, ultrasound waves are applied across my face to improve the skin’s elasticity and circulation, followed by microcurrent muscle stimulation during which I literally feel my cells awakening. The procedure soothes my mind so much I fall into a contented sleep. It’s all designed to boost my complexion’s glow—and it works. Dior’s global spa director, Olivier Hahn, told me he’s most proud of the sonic component of the spa offering, which does its job by calming me down without me even noticing.

A heavenly breakfast in my top-floor suite

The best kind of antioxidants at Oro restaurant

I wake up for the next stage of the treatment, a technical jaw massage, which the facialist carries out to counteract my nighttime teeth-grinding. She then places cryogenic stones over a cooling mask to firm, drain, and reoxygenate my skin. It’s a perfect way to re-enter the world, cognitively and physically. I feel snatched as I sip coffee by the pool after the treatment. The Mascarade facial is great for a morning-after depuffing, but, given the OMGs I receive from fellow spa-goers, I conclude that it’s also perfect for an evening out. I head out into the Venetian night with nothing but a touch of mascara and a post-facial luminosity.

Feeling like a kid on Christmas morning, the staff sent me on my way with a bag of the Dior Prestige products to keep up my skincare routine back home. The ingredients are mainly organic, something I hadn’t expected. In the same way that historic French vineyards downplay their organic practices for fear of alienating clients disdainful of natural wines, Dior also keeps its products' natural roots on the down low. It all comes as a pleasant surprise and further cements this spa’s authority in the world of regenerative beauty therapy.

#6277. Aer Lingus Unveils Business Class Suites With Doors And Its First Premium Economy Cabin On A330s

Aer Lingus has announced a cabin overhaul for 10 Airbus A330 aircraft, with the first refurbished jet scheduled to enter service on October 1, 2027. The initial route will be Dublin–New York JFK, on select EI104/EI105 services. Additional North American routes will follow as more aircraft are refurbished.

This is an A330-only project for now: there will be no corresponding cabin overhaul for the Airbus A321LR or A321XLR.

The refurbished aircraft will feature 28 Collins Elevation business class suites in a 1-2-1 layout. Every passenger will have direct aisle access and a closing door, with each seat converting into a 78-inch flat bed. Improved bedding and amenity kits are also planned.

The renderings look attractive to me. Green upholstery and lighter finishes give the cabin an Irish identity and a premium feel (hello Singapore Airlines). More importantly, the layout addresses a weakness I encountered on my Aer Lingus A330-200 flight from Dublin to Los Angeles. I had a window seat with a passenger beside me and no direct aisle access. Storage was limited too.

I slept well, but the seat was behind what many competitors offered. The lovely crew helped redeem that flight, though warm service should complement a competitive seat rather than compensate for one. Doors are fine, but giving every passenger access to the aisle is the more consequential improvement.

Aer Lingus also plans refreshed dining and a self-service business class snack and refreshment bar, much like SAS offers its on its A330 aircraft:

The new premium economy cabin will have four rows of Recaro R4 seats:

Passengers will receive an upgraded three-course meal, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones. It’s a hardly a unique or transformative hard product compared to its peers, but it’s an increasingly important middle way providing a noticeably more comfortable seat at a price that makes sense relative to economy and business class.

This fills an obvious gap for Aer Lingus. Someone who wants more room than economy offers but cannot justify a business class fare currently has limited options within the airline’s own cabin lineup. A genuine premium economy product gives that passenger another reason to stay with Aer Lingus.

Economy will retain the A330’s appealing 2-4-2 layout, with new seats and adjustable headrests. A self-service snack station is coming to this cabin too.

If I fly economy class, I prefer the A330 or 767. Two seats together by the window remain a compelling reason to choose an A330 when traveling as a couple, especially compared with being part of a block of three on most other widebody aircraft.

Aer Lingus promises more personal space, but we will wait for the final seat pitch and total economy seat count before drawing conclusions about legroom. A redesigned seatback can improve knee clearance without increasing the distance between rows, but padding is also essential.

The refurbished A330s will receive Panasonic Astrova entertainment systems, with 4K screens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and USB-C charging.

Free Starlink Wi-Fi will also be available, though Aer Lingus says that service is already offered across its transatlantic routes. Passengers do not need to wait for the new cabins to benefit from it. My previous A330 flight featured an entertainment system with missing graphics and internet that was slow but stable. Working screens and fast connectivity would improve the experience considerably.

For a daytime transatlantic flight, I place enormous value on reliable internet. A better seat may help me sleep on the overnight journey to Dublin, but Starlink makes the flight home a far more useful part of my day.

The first aircraft is still almost a year away, and the announcement does not provide a completion date for all 10 retrofits.

An October 1 launch on select JFK flights should not be confused with every Aer Lingus A330 having the new cabins from that date, even to JFK. During the transition, you’ll be able to tell which aircraft have the new business class because that aircraft will also be selling premium economy seats.

I hope Aer Lingus makes the differences clear during booking and handles aircraft substitutions sensibly…

Aer Lingus is giving 10 A330s new business class suites, adding premium economy, and refreshing economy class, with the first aircraft scheduled to debut between Dublin and New York JFK in October 2027.

My last longhaul flight on Aer Lingus left me impressed by the crew but disappointed by parts of the onboard product. This overhaul addresses the seat and technology shortcomings that made me reluctant to seek out the airline. I look forward to trying it. Aer Lingus already showed me how pleasant its service can be. Pair that with a competitive seat and better catering, and I might go out of my way to book it again.

#6275. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6274. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6273. New York Liberty Star Jonquel Jones Unpacks a Trip Home to the Bahamas

When Jonquel Jones picks up the phone to chat with us at Condé Nast Traveler, she’s in the back of her team bus, having just arrived in Minneapolis with the New York Liberty. In two days, she and her teammates will make WNBA history, defeating the Minnesota Lynx in Game 1 of the 2026 Playoffs. Their win will be the first time a No. 8 seed—the lowest-ranked team to qualify for the playoffs—beats a No. 1 seed, the league’s top-ranked team. But for Jones, such a victory will hardly qualify as new territory.

The 32-year-old New York Liberty center has spent the better part of the last decade breaking records: She has taken home all four major MVP honors, became the first international player named All-Star MVP, and helped lead the Liberty to their first-ever championship in 2024.

An athletic career like hers means rarely staying in one place for long—a reality reflected in the setting of our conversation. Between WNBA seasons and stints playing overseas, Jones has built a life where traveling has become a part of the game (off the court, of course). But no matter how far basketball takes her, there’s one destination that brings her back to herself: her home country, the Bahamas.

When her schedule finally allows for a pause, returning to the islands offers Jones a different kind of home-court advantage—and a chance to reconnect with the places and people that matter most to her. We caught up with the WNBA All-Star to talk through a typical trip back to the Bahamas, from the comforts she packs before leaving New York City and her in-flight essentials to the Bahamian delicacy she never returns without—plus how to make it yourself!

What trip are you unpacking for us?A trip to Grand Bahama, where I grew up.

Tell us about the itinerary: Where did you stay? What were the highlights?I always stay at my condo, which is close to where my family lives. I have homes both in the Bahamas and in New York. My grandmother, parents, cousins, nieces, and nephews are all still on the island. Aside from two of my siblings, pretty much my entire family still lives in the Bahamas, so getting to spend time with them is really special.

How often do you visit?I try to go back whenever I can, but it all depends on my schedule. This year’s off-season gives me a few months off, so I’ll be spending at least two months back home. During the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, though, I was only able to go for seven days. It really varies from year to year.

Who were you traveling with?I always bring my dog Rylo with me when I go back home. He’s a seven-year-old poodle mix, and he loves the Bahamas. I got him in 2019, right before COVID. I grew up around a lot of dogs—mostly yard dogs—and I’ve always had a special connection with animals.

Growing up, I had a dog named Princess, and she was my dog, for real—no pun intended. She went everywhere with me. Whether I was riding over to my grandmother’s house, walking to the beach, or playing basketball, she was always right there. She’d sit on the sidelines and watch me play, making sure I was okay. Princess was my first experience with unconditional love, and she’s the reason I fell in love with dogs.

On this trip, did you overpack, underpack, or get it just right?I’m definitely an overpacker. I like bringing little comforts from home in New York, like my favorite matcha and coffee beans. I’m a big matcha fan, so I’ll even bring my entire matcha set. There’s a Japanese market called Midoriya Japanese Grocery on Fifth Avenue in Brooklyn that has amazing matcha, and I always stock up before a trip. I’m also a big fan of Stumptown Coffee; Hair Bender is my go-to blend. It’s nice to have a few pieces of my everyday routine with me. They help me settle in.

What drugstore essentials do you always have in your backpack?Claritin! I have to have it with me. I have terrible allergies, and something about the pine trees in the Bahamas make them go crazy. I actually recently brought a friend back home with me, and the two of us spent the entire trip passing the bottle back and forth. Without my Claritin, it definitely takes me longer to acclimate.

What is a little luxury you always bring with you?A nighttime face mask. I love having something I can use to pamper myself during a little girls’ night in. A good overnight mask is my go-to when I want to firm up my skin or wake up with a little extra glow.

Do you have a favorite item of travel clothing to fly in?Comfort is definitely my priority when I travel. I'm not just looking after myself, but Rylo, too, so I want to make sure we're both comfortable. Dogs can pick up on nervous energy, and I don't want him to sense that from me. I try to stay in a relaxed, zen state so we can both enjoy the trip.I'm a Nike athlete, and I love their top and bottom sets. They have great two-piece options that are simple but fashionable, which makes them perfect for traveling.

What's one piece of home you always pack?I’m probably going to sound crazy, but I’m a gamer, and bringing my PlayStation 5 console is a big part of how I get comfortable and settle in when I get back to the Bahamas. I have a whole gaming setup waiting for me at my condo, so all I have to do is plug in my PS5 and I’m ready to go. It’s one item I never travel home without.

What's your go-to snack to keep on hand for long travel days?It’s probably not the healthiest choice, but I grew up eating Cadbury Crunchie Bars. I loved them as a kid, then went through a phase where I stopped eating them. For some reason, though, I’ve recently fallen back in love with them, and they’ve become my go-to. Now they also make Cadbury Crunchie Rocks, which are bite-size, cluster versions of the bar that come in a resealable bag, making them a little easier to travel with. I also love Cadbury Dairy Milk Fruit & Nut. Oh my god, that bar? So good. I feel a little like a granny saying this, but it’s one of my favorites. It has almonds, raisins, and dried fruit—it's delicious. My mom used to buy it when I was growing up, and as a kid, I couldn't understand why she liked it so much. But, lo and behold, I get it now.

What's your in-flight routine like?I’d say either my Steam Deck, a portable gaming system, or a good book. I’m a big reader and use it to escape. I especially love fiction and fantasy. I recently read The Sword of Kaigen: A Theonite War Story, which has a similar feel to Avatar: The Last Airbender. It’s such a great book, but fair warning: the fight scenes are brutal, so prepare yourself. It’s worth it, though.I also can’t travel without my Bose headphones. Those are an absolute must.

What's a fragrance that never leave home without?I love, love, love the LV Lovers fragrance by Pharrell Williams in collaboration with Louis Vuitton.

Last question: What souvenirs do you bring home?Whenever I leave the Bahamas, I always bring back conch. It’s a Bahamian delicacy that you’ll find in every dish, and can be prepared in so many different ways. My favorite is conch fritters, made by tenderizing the conch and mixing it into a batter with onions, thyme, and celery.I always bring back bags of frozen conch fritter batter so I can enjoy a taste of home once I'm back in the United States. Whenever I'm craving them, I just thaw the batter, add a little baking powder, and deep-fry it. And just like that, I have fresh conch fritters. The closest comparison I can make is a hush puppy. If you can't find conch, you could probably try making them with calamari, too.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6272. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#6271. Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

World of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

Hyatt has announced changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

Globalists currently receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

Hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

“This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”

After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

The ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

That addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to plan a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

For someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

There are still restrictions. For example, the new Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

Some milestone free night certificates currently expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very quickly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

But Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards currently can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

Here are some notable new choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):

The $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

At 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking…

The new Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice new update.

The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

But the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

Maldives, Paris, London, New York, Milan, Tokyo, Any SE Asia property are all examples of Park Hyatts (which comprise the most percentage of aspirational hotels) and for which I imagine Hyatt’s number is conservative – betting parking comprises less than 5% of total check-ins on points. I do feel bad for you that you got a concierge that is less than helpful, but it’s not the case across the board. I have had two over the past ten years and both have been amazing. They respond by email during working hours in minutes and have handled some unusual requests for me just wonderfully. I guess my point being that if it’s so bad with yours (and I know Ben says the same on OMAAT about his) I’m at a loss at why you don’t start sending out emails as such to get a new one assigned. Mine were all horrible too, but I have heard of some great ones…

I personally wish they’d get rid of the club passes since it seems that most properties I’ve been to sinve covid have closed them. I’d prefer free breakfast vouchers for the years I come up short of globalist.

I think the club lounge passes or certificates — whatever they are called — are a complete scam since the vast majority of Hyatt Regency and Grand Hyatt properties, at least in the United States, no longer have an open or operational club lounge.

It would be nice if they were Club Access and/or Free Breakfast certificates…

#6270. Meeks vows Iran votes as he seeks Foreign Affairs gavel

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and staffers cheer as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., takes the stage during a election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress's constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can't tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”

#6269. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.
